caption:
Meta's carbon footprint rose 45% in 2025 as it built out AI data centers.
The company now says it is re-evaluating its goal of net zero by 2030.
New gas plants for its data centers are not even in that number yet.

Should AI companies drop climate goals to build faster?

threads_text: Meta's emissions jumped 45% in one year from its AI buildout, and it now says its 2030 net zero goal is up for review. Google, Amazon and Microsoft say they are sticking with theirs. Is net zero by 2030 still realistic for any AI company?

site_article.headline: Meta reviews its 2030 net zero goal after emissions rise 45 percent
site_article.dek: The company's carbon footprint grew sharply in 2025 as it added AI data centers, and new gas plants built for those sites are not yet in the count.
site_article.summary: Meta said it is re-evaluating its goal of reaching net zero emissions by 2030 after its net carbon footprint rose 45 percent in 2025. The increase followed a 35 percent jump in electricity use tied to new data centers.
site_article.seo_title: Meta reviews 2030 net zero goal as AI emissions rise 45%
site_article.seo_description: Meta's net carbon footprint rose 45% in 2025 to 11.9 million tons as AI data centers grew, and the company says it is re-evaluating its 2030 net zero goal.
site_article.answer_summary: Meta has not dropped its 2030 net zero goal, but its executives say they are re-evaluating the timeline after the company's net emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 during its AI data center buildout.
site_article.hero_alt: The Meta sign at the entrance to the company's headquarters campus.

paragraphs.text: Meta is reconsidering its pledge to reach net zero emissions across its value chain by 2030, after its net carbon footprint rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to its latest sustainability report as described by Trellis and Axios on November 19, 2026.

The company first announced the 2030 goal in 2020, when it still operated under the Facebook name and before the current wave of generative AI investment, Axios reported. In the report, Rachel Peterson, Meta's vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that the company is re-evaluating its timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 date and near-term intensity targets.

The executives did not say what changes they are considering or when a decision will come. According to Trellis, they committed only to share the outcome of that review later. They wrote that "the reality has been far more complex" than the steady growth and falling clean energy costs they had expected, Axios reported.

Meta's electricity use rose 35 percent in 2025, driven by new data centers, and electricity related emissions grew almost 38 percent from 2024, Trellis reported. The figure of 11.9 million tons counts contractual instruments such as clean energy purchases. Measured by the grid where its facilities actually sit, the location based total was 21.7 million tons.

Most of the increase came from the company's supply chain. Emissions from purchased goods and services rose 36 percent and emissions from capital goods rose 58 percent, according to Trellis. Meta's cumulative indirect, or Scope 3, emissions now stand more than 105 percent above 2021 levels, even though one of its supporting goals is to keep them at or below 2021 levels by 2030. A separate target calls for a 42 percent cut in operational and purchased electricity emissions by 2030.

Meta's operational emissions have fallen each year since 2021, and the company has matched all of its electricity use with clean and renewable energy since 2020, Trellis reported. Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal power, but less than half of that capacity is producing electricity so far, according to Axios. Trellis pointed to long grid interconnection and permitting queues, along with slow supply chains for low carbon building materials, as reasons clean energy projects have stalled.

The report says Meta may turn to natural gas plants where utilities cannot deliver power quickly enough, and some of those projects are already underway, Axios reported. In Louisiana, the utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas fired units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts for Meta's data centers. Ohio regulators approved a 200 megawatt gas plant built for Meta, and the research firm Cleanview has identified a 521 megawatt gas project under construction for the company in Utah. None of these plants are reflected in the 45 percent figure.

Meta's direct water consumption fell 4 percent, but consumption in highly water stressed regions rose 24 percent, and water used to generate its electricity rose 37 percent before clean energy purchases, according to Axios. Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, credited Meta with being the only large technology company to disclose the water tied to its electricity, Axios reported.

Other large technology companies also reported higher emissions: Microsoft's rose 25 percent, Google's 18 percent and Amazon's 16 percent. According to Trellis, all three say they are keeping their climate pledges, which makes Meta the first of the four to say it will reconsider its timeline.

The report shows how quickly an AI infrastructure buildout can overtake a climate plan written for a different era of computing. Meta's clean energy contracts are large on paper, but the gap between contracted and operating capacity, plus new gas plants that have not yet entered the inventory, suggests the reported emissions may not have peaked.
The next marker is Meta's revised timeline and whether it sets new interim targets, along with how much of the Louisiana, Ohio and Utah gas capacity appears in its next emissions report.
